messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Priya Patel was 44 when she came to treatment, a married South Asian American woman who had spent years working on the sales floor of a large retail store, where she was known as reliable, agreeable, and calm with difficult customers. The event she described happened at work. One afternoon, during a busy shift, a woman near the front of the store suddenly collapsed. Priya saw the fall, heard the sickening sound of the woman hitting the floor, and watched the confusion that followed as people shouted for help. Someone began crying loudly; another customer froze; an employee called 911. Priya stayed nearby long enough to see the woman lying motionless and to register the fear on the faces around her, but afterward what remained was not a tidy narrative. She could recall fragments—the woman’s body on the floor, the sound of crying, her own lightheadedness, the rush of people—but when she tried to tell it straight through, the sequence slipped away from her. She would stop mid-sentence, unsure what had happened first and what had come after.

In the days that followed, Priya found that certain moments reached back into that afternoon with startling force. If she heard someone cry, especially in a public place, her chest tightened and she felt unsteady, as if the floor might tilt under her. When she became dizzy or lightheaded for any reason, even briefly, it frightened her because it felt too close to how her body had felt while she was standing near the woman on the ground. Even being asked about the incident could undo her. Coworkers initially spoke about it in the break room in the practical way people do after something frightening happens, but as soon as Priya tried to join in, she became overwhelmed. The memories came back not as a clear story but as broken, emotionally loaded pieces, and with them came a wave of grief so strong she had to stop talking. What struck her was not just fear but sorrow; she found herself carrying the image of that woman and feeling a heavy, immediate grief whenever the memory surfaced.

Over the following months, Priya became noticeably more watchful. At work she scanned the entrances, the aisles, customers’ faces, and the space near the registers, as if danger might declare itself in some small sign before anyone else noticed. If a cart rattled unexpectedly behind her or a voice rose suddenly over the store music, she jumped. She began positioning herself where she could see more of the floor. When a customer started to look unwell, or when there was any commotion, she felt herself become intensely alert, almost braced. This constant searching for signs of trouble followed her outside the store as well, in parking lots, grocery lines, and family outings. She was certain she needed to stay on guard.

Priya also found herself turning the event over in her mind, asking why it had happened to her, why she had been the one standing there, why that afternoon had lodged itself so deeply when other people seemed to move on. She did not arrive at satisfying answers, but the questions returned repeatedly. In her relationships, particularly at work, she became even more inclined to go along with what others wanted. If a manager asked her to switch stations or stay in a busier area, she agreed quickly. If a customer was demanding, she gave in where she could. This made sense to her as a way to keep things calm and avoid any scene that might escalate into distress around her. Over time, though, it left her more depleted. Her husband noticed that she came home exhausted and withdrawn, and that if he gently asked what was wrong, she would sometimes start to speak, then abruptly stop, tearful and overcome.

By the time she sought help, Priya felt her world had narrowed around anticipation and interruption. She could still do her job, but every shift involved scanning, bracing, and trying not to be caught off guard. The store, once familiar, had become a place where crying customers, sudden noise, or her own momentary dizziness could pull her back into the worst fragments of that day. She was distressed by how little control she had when the memory returned, and by the fact that she still could not put the event in order despite having thought about it so often. What finally brought her in was a recent incident at work when a customer began crying near the registers and Priya immediately felt overwhelmed and lightheaded, needing to step away before she could continue. She said she was afraid that if this kept happening she would not be able to function at work or talk to her family about what she had been carrying. More than anything, she hoped for a way to remember what happened without being overtaken by grief each time it came back.
